title: Biological contamination and incident escalation
audience: Pool cleaners and technicians who may be called to a pool after an illness, injury or contamination event, in any state or territory
learningOutcomes: Recognise signs of biological contamination in pool water and on surfaces
Take the first protective actions: keep people out of the water, notify the operator, and use PPE
Escalate according to the operator's emergency plan and not make a reopening decision
Record the event, the actions and the people informed

instruction.heading: Recognising a biological incident
instruction.body: Biological contamination in a pool may be visible or suspected. Examples include faecal matter, vomit, blood, and an unexplained illness reported by swimmers. A serious injury or a drowning event is a different and more urgent emergency. Treat every suspected contamination as a risk to people in the water and to the people cleaning up. Do not assume that the water is safe because it looks clear.

instruction.heading: First protective actions
instruction.body: The first priority is the people. Stop the task. Make sure swimmers leave the water and that the pool area is controlled, following the operator's plan. Call the emergency number if someone is seriously injured or unwell. Notify the responsible operator or duty manager straight away. Do not enter the water to remove material while swimmers are present. Put on the PPE set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}} before any direct contact, and keep others away from the area while you work.

instruction.heading: What you must not decide
instruction.body: The operator decides on closure and reopening under the operator plan and the applicable public-health rules. Requirements for responding to a contamination event are set by state and territory authorities. Do not dose the pool to 'fix' the water, and do not tell customers or swimmers that the pool is safe to use. Treating the water is a water-treatment decision that requires the operator's plan and instruction (see the pool chemistry lessons, “Disinfection chemistry and pH interpretation” and “Dosing systems and chlorine-gas prevention”).

instruction.heading: Cleaning up within scope
instruction.body: Where the work order and the operator plan allow it, remove visible material from deck surfaces and equipment with disposable tools, bag and seal the waste as the site waste procedure directs, and disinfect contaminated equipment and surfaces using products approved for the site. Keep contaminated equipment separate from clean equipment. Large or complex biological contamination, or any body fluid cleanup beyond pool surrounds, is outside this lesson. Refer it to the operator and to the High-risk cleaning module, where that scope applies.

instruction.heading: Exposure and records
instruction.body: If you come into contact with pool water or body fluid, wash the area, report it to your supervisor as the site incident procedure directs, and seek medical advice if the operator or your supervisor advises it. Record the event with the time, the number of people in the water, what you observed, the actions you took, and who you told. Do not record a guess about the cause as a fact.

procedure: Stop the task and make sure no one is in the water.
Call the emergency number if anyone is seriously injured or unwell.
Notify the responsible operator or duty manager immediately.
Put on PPE as set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}} before any direct contact.
Keep others away from the area and the water until the operator decides.
Remove visible material only if the work order and plan allow it; bag and seal the waste as the site procedure directs.
Disinfect equipment and surfaces only with approved products and per the site plan.
Record the time, people in the water, observations, actions and people informed.

workedExamples.situation: During a clean at a hotel pool, a guest reports a diarrhoea incident in the water. The cleaner is about to start skimming.
workedExamples.reasoning: The cleaner stops and does not skim or enter the water. Swimmers are asked to leave under the operator's plan. The duty manager is told at once. The cleaner records the time, the number of people in the water and what was observed, and waits for the operator's closure and treatment decision.

workedExamples.situation: A supervisor tells a cleaner to finish the job quickly and tells the cleaner that adding more chlorine will fix the problem.
workedExamples.reasoning: The cleaner does not treat the water without the operator's plan and instruction. The cleaner explains that closure and treatment are the operator's decision, asks the supervisor for written instruction, and records the instruction and the decision.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved disinfectant for surfaces and equipment

commonErrors.error: Continuing to clean while swimmers are in the water.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop the task and have swimmers leave under the operator's plan.

commonErrors.error: Dosing the water without the operator's plan or instruction.
commonErrors.prevention: Notify the operator and wait for the treatment decision.

commonErrors.error: Telling customers or swimmers that the pool is safe.
commonErrors.prevention: Only the operator decides on use. Record what was observed.

commonErrors.error: Storing contaminated equipment with clean equipment.
commonErrors.prevention: Bag, separate and clean contaminated equipment per the site procedure.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Contaminated pool water and body fluids are biological hazards. Wear PPE, keep people out of the water, and wash after any contact.
Requirements for responding to pool contamination events and for reopening are set by state and territory authorities. Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan.
Large or complex biological contamination, or body fluid cleanup beyond pool surrounds, is treated here as outside scope. Refer it to the High-risk cleaning module.

qualityStandard: Swimmers are out of the water and the operator is notified before any cleaning starts
The worker does not make or imply a reopening decision
The incident record has times, people, observations, actions and people informed
documentationEvidence: Incident record with time and people in the water
Actions taken and the person informed
Equipment and surfaces disinfected, with products used
summary: People first: stop the task, get swimmers out, and call for help if needed.
The operator decides on closure, treatment and reopening.
Use PPE for any direct contact; separate contaminated equipment.
Record what was observed and what was done, not guesses about cause.

knowledgeChecks.question: During a pool clean, a swimmer reports a suspected faecal incident in the water. What is the first action?
options: Start skimming the water to remove the debris first before anything
Stop the task, get swimmers out of the water, and notify the operator
Tell the swimmer the pool is safe to use again today and the water is clean
Dose the pool heavily to clear the water quickly and fully today

knowledgeChecks.question: Who decides when a contaminated pool may be reopened?
options: The cleaning contractor who is working at the pool on the day
The swimmer who reported the incident in the water this morning
The operator, under the operator plan and applicable public-health rules
The chemical supplier who delivered the product to the site on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the correct handling of contaminated cleaning equipment?
options: Store it with clean equipment to save space in the shed
Bag, separate and clean it according to the site procedure
Rinse it in the clean pool water before the next job
Use it on the next pool without cleaning it first today
